# aircraftdefects.com

> 1,757,827 service difficulty reports filed with the US Federal Aviation
> Administration between 1 January 1995 and 26 August 2026, on 54,634 aircraft,
> made readable. Each report records a defect a mechanic found. The FAA publishes
> them as coded rows; this site decodes the codes from the FAA's own lookup
> tables and has GLM-5.3-Flash read the mechanic's free-text write-up and restate
> it in plain English, with the original always shown alongside.

Built by Henk van Ess, a Digital Digging site: https://www.digitaldigging.org
Source and method: https://github.com/voelspriet/aircraftdefects

## What this data is, and is not

- A report is filed when a mechanic finds a failure, malfunction or defect. Filing
  is the maintenance system working, not failing.
- Counts here are counts of reports filed. They are not counts of incidents, and
  they are not accidents. The file records no accidents.
- The file records no causes. Nothing on this site says why anything happened.
- The FAA file carries no fleet sizes and no flying hours, so no rate can be
  computed from it. This site computes none and publishes no safety ranking of
  airlines or aircraft types. A large airline files more reports because it flies
  more aircraft more hours, and a rigorous maintenance department files more than
  a careless one.
- Airline names are decoded from the FAA's December 2006 designator
  cross-reference and can be stale. Check current ownership before publishing.
- Location is recorded as a numbered zone. ZONE 700 is the landing gear. About
  85% of reports describe the location in words instead and carry no zone code;
  the site says how many it cannot place rather than drawing only what it can.
- Single letters are reused across the form. `A` in one column means the crew made
  an unscheduled landing; `A` elsewhere means an airline filed the report.

## How the model is used

- Every quote the model makes is checked by the server against the record it
  cites, as a literal substring, before it is shown. A sentence whose quote fails
  is deleted and the page prints how many were checked and how many survived.
- The model is asked to state what the file cannot answer before it answers.
- The words because, caused, led to and due to are forbidden in its output,
  because the file records no causes.
- Nothing generated is shown without the filer's own words beside it and a record
  number under it.

## Pages

- https://aircraftdefects.com/ : the tool
- https://aircraftdefects.com/conflicts/ : reports where the coded box disagrees
  with the sentence the same mechanic wrote underneath it
- https://aircraftdefects.com/z/case/<control number> : one report on its own
  page, every code spelled out, built for citing
- https://aircraftdefects.com/z/rebuilt : the earlier interface, written whole by
  GLM-5.3-Flash from written specifications, kept for comparison

## Where the data comes from

The FAA publishes one CSV per year at
https://external.apic4e.faa.gov/sdrs/retrieve/SDR-<year>.csv, 1995 to the present.
There is no API; the files are downloaded whole and rebuilt here. The FAA's own
search over the same data is at https://sdrs.faa.gov and its code tables are at
https://sdrs.faa.gov/References.aspx. The aircraft registry is a separate daily
file at https://registry.faa.gov/database/ReleasableAircraft.zip.

The NTSB accident file is a different agency's record, published monthly at
https://data.ntsb.gov/avdata and beginning in January 2008. A case page shows
any NTSB cases on that tail number, clearly separated. The two files are never
merged: an NTSB case explains nothing in the maintenance record and the
maintenance record explains nothing about the case.

## Citing

Cite the FAA record number, which every page carries, and the FAA's own system at
https://sdrs.faa.gov as the source. The data is a work of the US government and is
in the public domain. This site is MIT licensed.
